content:
Astronomers have discovered 47 faint dwarf galaxy candidates that could help reveal the secrets of dark matter

An international team of astronomers has identified 47 candidate dwarf galaxies around three larger galaxies, uncovering a hidden population of extremely faint cosmic objects. The discovery could help scientists test existing theories about galaxy formation, the role of dark matter and the evolution of the Universe.

Dwarf galaxies are the most common type of galaxy in the Universe, but their low luminosity makes them extremely difficult to detect. For this reason, the faintest are sometimes referred to as “ghost galaxies”. Most known dwarf galaxies have so far been discovered relatively close to the Milky Way, while astronomers continue to struggle to explain the number and distribution of such objects around larger host galaxies.

Early observations revealed fewer satellite galaxies than predicted by computer simulations. This phenomenon is known as the “missing satellites problem”. More recent studies, however, have sometimes indicated the opposite trend.

To determine whether similar patterns can be observed beyond the Milky Way’s immediate cosmic neighbourhood, the international team focused on regions around three galaxies - NGC 5068, NGC 5084 and NGC 5087 - located approximately 17 million, 80 million and 100 million light-years from Earth, respectively.

The scientists used the VST telescope at the European Southern Observatory’s Paranal Observatory in Chile. The resulting images are the deepest optical observations of these regions to date. Rather than relying on automated software, three researchers examined the images manually to reduce the likelihood of extremely faint objects being missed.

The team identified a total of 47 dwarf galaxy candidates, only four of which were known before the study. Their colours and shapes suggest that they could indeed be dwarf galaxies, although further observations are needed to confirm their distances and motions.

Some of the candidates have no clearly defined internal structure and may be elliptical or spheroidal dwarf galaxies, while others show structures characteristic of spiral or irregular galaxies. Their estimated masses range from around one million to one billion times the mass of the Sun.

The scientists note that some of the candidates around NGC 5084 may be arranged in a flat structure similar to that observed among satellite galaxies around the Milky Way. However, additional data will be needed to confirm this pattern.

Future spectroscopic observations, as well as forthcoming surveys by the European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope, are expected to help determine whether the identified objects are genuinely orbiting the three larger galaxies and whether additional, as yet undiscovered dwarf galaxies exist. | BGNES
